Title: CrowdStrike Reportedly Paying $495 Million for AI Security Firms Fiddler, Dreadnode
Context: CrowdStrike on Tuesday announced agreements to acquire AI agent observability firm Fiddler AI and AI security testing company Dreadnode, in deals reportedly worth a combined...
Full Text:
CrowdStrike on Tuesday announced agreements to acquire AI agent observability firm Fiddler AI and AI security testing company Dreadnode, in deals reportedly worth a combined $495 million.

CrowdStrike has not disclosed the financial terms of either acquisition. According to The Wall Street Journal, which reported the deals ahead of the official announcements, the cybersecurity giant is paying roughly $400 million for Fiddler and about $95 million for Dreadnode.

CrowdStrike said both purchases will be paid mostly in cash, with a portion in stock subject to vesting conditions. The deals are expected to close in the fourth quarter of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2027, which ends on January 31, 2027.

Fiddler was founded in 2018 and is based in Palo Alto, California. In January, it announced a $30 million Series C round that brought its total funding to $100 million.

The company’s technology monitors AI agents and explains the decisions they make. CrowdStrike says Fiddler will add pre-deployment evaluation of agents, tracing of their reasoning and tool calls, and detection of behavioral drift and hallucinations in production.

It will also log agent activity for compliance audits and track token usage and spending. CrowdStrike plans to sell the technology as Falcon Observe.

Dreadnode, founded in 2023, develops offensive AI security tools. The startup raised $14 million in Series A funding in early 2025.

According to CrowdStrike, Dreadnode’s platform lets users describe in plain language what they want to test. It then runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks.

The tests target AI models, agent reasoning loops, applications and MCP servers. Findings are ranked by severity, mapped to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, MITRE ATLAS and the NIST AI RMF, and fed to CrowdStrike’s Falcon Guardian AI detection and response product as policy recommendations.

The Dreadnode team, led by CEO Brad Palm, will join CrowdStrike’s Cyber Superintelligence Lab. Dreadnode-based testing capabilities are expected to become generally available in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

Alongside the acquisitions, CrowdStrike introduced an AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian that allows authorized administrators to halt a misbehaving AI agent, prevent it from restarting, and cut off its network access.

CrowdStrike has made several security acquisitions over the past year. In January, it announced plans to buy identity security firm SGNL for $740 million and browser security company Seraphic for a reported $420 million. In September 2025, it agreed to acquire AI security firm Pangea.

Title: CrowdStrike Advances AI Security and Safety from Endpoint to Cloud
Context: OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they...
Full Text:
AI agents are transforming enterprise computing. What began with employees using AI assistants is evolving into autonomous agents that access enterprise resources, invoke tools, execute code, and take action at machine speed.

This introduces a new security and safety challenge. Organizations must protect agents from attacks while ensuring those agents operate safely and as intended. Security teams need to discover where agents operate, understand what they were instructed to do, trace their actions, and intervene when their behavior becomes dangerous.

Traditional security approaches provide only part of the picture. Endpoint runtime security monitors execution but lacks the AI-specific context needed to explain what triggered it. Network inspection can monitor AI communications but not the actions that agents take on systems. Agent-level integrations can inspect AI interactions but cannot reveal downstream execution.

At Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike unveiled innovations that advance AI detection and response (AIDR) across three critical dimensions: architecture, coverage, and controls. We also introduced a new AI kill switch for CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian that empowers security teams to rapidly cut off AI model access at AI gateways when agents become dangerous. And we shared the general availability of CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Guardian, which extends 24/7 managed detection and response to AI security.

The Right Architecture for Securing AI Agents

Securing AI agents requires visibility and control across three critical layers: OS-level runtime execution, network communications, and agent interactions. Falcon Guardian brings these layers together to connect what agents are instructed to do with what they execute.

OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they run, and resources they access. This visibility is not achievable directly via network inspection or per-agent hook integration approaches.

Endpoint network inspection extends visibility into agent communications (Pre-beta): CrowdStrike announced plans to expand this capability to macOS, where it will inspect traffic entering and leaving the endpoint to help security teams identify risky interactions.

Agent-level hooks provide direct inspection and policy enforcement within supported AI agents (Available now): Hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor enable organizations to inspect prompts and block malicious activity at the source, before harmful actions are executed.

Together, these three layers give Falcon Guardian visibility into agent instructions, communications, and runtime execution. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects this activity, linking what agents were instructed to do with what they actually executed and the resources they affected. This gives security teams the context to understand agent behavior, investigate threats, and trace their impact from prompt to process.

See it in action:

The Right Coverage: Secured AI Wherever It Operates

Falcon Guardian initially focused on securing workforce AI adoption and autonomous agents at the endpoint, where employees interact with AI and agents execute with user permissions.

Now, as enterprises build and deploy their own agents in production environments, CrowdStrike is expanding Falcon Guardian's AI-specific protections across more of the cloud infrastructure the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform already secures. Newly announced capabilities will extend Falcon Guardian coverage across Linux, cloud workloads, Kubernetes, and managed AI platforms.

Expanded cloud coverage (Pre-beta): On Linux, Falcon Guardian will bring agent discovery, visibility, and AI-specific detections to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. In cloud workloads and Kubernetes, Falcon Guardian will extend these capabilities to enterprise-developed AI agents and applications, including those built with LangChain and LangGraph. Using the Falcon Linux sensor, deployed directly or as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, Falcon Guardian will connect AI activity with surrounding runtime, workload, and identity context.

For provider-managed AI environments, Falcon Guardian will expand agent discovery and AI-layer visibility, beginning with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This will help security teams identify managed agents, understand their components and interactions, and assess AI-specific risks without requiring access to provider-controlled infrastructure.

Title: CrowdStrike to Acquire Fiddler to Deliver Falcon Observe for AI Agent Observability
Context: It will become part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform as CrowdStrike Falcon® Observe, generally available in Q4 FY27
Full Text:
I am delighted to announce CrowdStrike’s intent to acquire Fiddler at Fal.Con EU 2026. Fiddler, a leader in AI observability, will help ensure enterprise AI agents act as intended with pre-deployment evaluation and continuous behavioral monitoring as part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform.

Every business deploying AI agents asks the same questions: What are our agents doing? Are they staying on task? Are they acting in a way that could put the business at risk?

AI agents don’t have to be compromised to be dangerous. Those that stay within their guardrails can make a bad decision or take harmful action using valid credentials and approved enterprise tools. Businesses must be able to trace agents’ activity and explain anomalies as these concerns become top of mind among auditors, regulators, board members, and risk managers.

Enterprise AI safety requires a comprehensive approach: Evaluate agents before deployment, understand their decisions and actions, and continuously monitor their behavior. AI observability provides a lens into agent behavior before and after they ship. AI explainability shows why agents made their decisions and where their actions may have gone awry.

Fiddler delivers both. It will become part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform as CrowdStrike Falcon® Observe, generally available in Q4 FY27. With this acquisition, CrowdStrike will extend our AI security capabilities beyond protecting AI systems into proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day.

Building AI Trust in the Agentic Enterprise

Unlike traditional software, AI agents can make autonomous decisions, invoke tools, and take actions across enterprise systems. If software can act autonomously, security needs a record of those actions: what each agent decided, how it acted, what it changed, and the tools it used. They must know whether the agent made the correct decisions to follow its intended task.

As an example: Consider an AI agent using approved tools and valid credentials to process a customer refund. The agent makes an incorrect decision and approves a refund that violates company policy. Traditional security controls may see legitimate activity, but AI explainability reveals why the agent made that decision and where its behavior went wrong.

Fiddler provides AI observability for the agentic era. It helps organizations identify misaligned agents before they are deployed and continues to monitor agent behavior post-deployment so businesses have full visibility into what they’re doing and why.

Before deployment, teams can compare prompts, models, and configurations to evaluate whether agents perform intended tasks safely and accurately before they reach production.

After deployment, teams can trace agents’ decisions and reasoning paths across the full agent hierarchy to detect issues like behavioral drift and unintended actions before they cause harm. Fiddler reconstructs the agent’s decision-making process so teams can trace each failure to the step that caused it.

Fiddler supports auditable AI governance across organizations’ existing agents and tools. Its granular view of agents’ decision-making covers first-party and third-party agents across the enterprise so teams have the data they need to support compliance and audits. Businesses also gain explainability across the frameworks they run, as Fiddler enables teams to instrument agents through OpenTelemetry and supports LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands, and Google ADK.

As part of the Falcon platform, Fiddler will connect AI agent intent and behavior with Falcon security telemetry across endpoints, identity, cloud, and runtime environments. This will help security teams understand why an agent took an action and what happened across the enterprise as a result. By connecting agent decisions with enterprise security context, CrowdStrike will provide visibility that goes beyond standalone AI observability.

CrowdStrike Delivers the Enterprise AI Control Plane

This milestone extends CrowdStrike’s leadership in protecting the agentic enterprise. Our acquisition of Fiddler, together with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian innovations announced today, will bring comprehensive AI security and safety solutions to the Falcon platform.

CrowdStrike can already establish AI agents as trusted identities, connect those identities to the humans operating them, grant access to business systems based on real-time risk, and secure AI agents at runtime. Fiddler will extend the Falcon platform to the earliest stages of the agent lifecycle, before deployment, to monitor their behavior before and after production, and explain the decisions they make.

Falcon Guardian protects AI agents from attacks and misuse. Falcon Observe evaluates and explains whether agents behave as intended. Together, they secure AI operations in the agentic enterprise.

There are a number of risks that could cause actual results to differ materially, including the satisfaction of the acquisition’s closing conditions, our ability to integrate Fiddler, and other risks described in the filings we make with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission from time to time.

Title: Introducing AI Kill Switch: Taking Control When AI Agents Go Rogue
Context: The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches
Full Text:
One Kill Switch with Comprehensive Enforcement Points

Coming soon, CrowdStrike will extend AI Kill Switch beyond gateway enforcement to deliver coordinated agent containment across the Falcon platform.

AI agents operate across endpoints, cloud environments, SaaS applications, browsers, and enterprise identities, often spanning multiple environments in a single chain of activity. When an agent goes rogue, stopping it shouldn't require security teams to investigate and respond separately in every environment.

CrowdStrike's vision is one AI Kill Switch coordinating response across multiple enforcement points. This will bring together the security capabilities of the Falcon platform and its broader ecosystem to contain rogue agents wherever they operate, including:

Endpoint agents: Terminate rogue agents and associated processes directly on affected endpoints and prevent them from restarting.

Cloud agents: Contain or terminate compromised agents operating in cloud environments.

User and agent identities: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen Identity Security to revoke agent permissions at runtime and restrict access to enterprise resources.

SaaS agents: Extend containment through CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield to restrict or terminate agent activity within SaaS environments.

Browser sessions: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser to terminate sessions and disrupt unauthorized activity through web applications.

This evolution will enable increasingly targeted containment so security teams can stop individual rogue agents or groups of agents with surgical precision while minimizing disruption to business operations.

CrowdStrike's architectural advantage goes beyond individual enforcement mechanisms. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects AI intent to downstream execution, revealing what an agent was asked to do, what it did, and which systems or resources were affected. This context helps security teams understand the threat and determine where to intervene. CrowdStrike Charlotte Agentic SOAR provides the no-code security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) capabilities to coordinate enforcement across the Falcon platform, enabling automated AI Kill Switch workflows triggered by AI-specific detections or risky agent behavior.

Rather than responding to isolated events through disconnected tools, security teams will be able to coordinate containment across the agentic attack surface.

Secure AI Adoption Without Losing Control

AI agents are becoming a powerful part of enterprise operations. As their autonomy and reach expand, organizations need security that can keep pace.

With AI Kill Switch, CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges. This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.

The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches.

Title: CrowdStrike Secures AI Agents Inside Claude Cowork
Context: Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent...
Full Text:
When Claude Cowork executes code locally, it runs inside an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer. On the host, that VM runs as a single opaque process: The agent's activity inside the VM, including the processes it spawns, the packages it installs, and the network connections it makes, is not visible to the host's endpoint security sensor. Because host folders can be mounted into the VM, sensitive data can sit within the agent's reach.

Today at Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike announced it is bringing CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian protection natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution. It runs the Falcon sensor directly inside the Cowork VM on both macOS and Windows to bring runtime visibility and detection into the agent's execution environment.

The integration is now available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November.

How It Works

Consider this scenario: A user asks Cowork for a script to align their slides to a brand standard. While completing the task, the agent installs the latest version of a common Python package. Neither the user nor the agent knows that an adversary has compromised the package at its source. Once installed, that package reads host data through a mounted folder and sends it out to a known malicious endpoint. The Falcon sensor running inside the VM would detect it. This is exactly the type of malicious activity and potential data exfiltration the integration is built to detect as agents execute tasks.

CrowdStrike’s sensor integration with the Cowork VM will deliver:

Visibility and detection where agents execute: Process, package, and network activity inside the Cowork VM will no longer be a blind spot, so teams can detect and investigate threats with the same Falcon telemetry they use everywhere else.

The same visibility on macOS and Windows: The VM runs the same Linux environment on both, so customers get consistent coverage regardless of the OS.

Deployment and control through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform: Admins will turn the integration on through their existing device management, the same way they deploy the Falcon sensor today, and the Falcon Linux sensor deploys inside the Cowork VM. From there, the team controls it through the Falcon platform so Claude Cowork comes under the same security control plane as the rest of the environment.

Built with Anthropic

CrowdStrike and Anthropic worked together to bring Falcon protection directly into Claude Cowork's execution environment. Anthropic enabled Falcon deployment within Cowork, while CrowdStrike engineered and tested the integration across installation, real-time protection, and ongoing updates. Through this beta integration, enterprises can extend the security they already trust from the Falcon platform to AI agents in Claude Cowork, alongside the virtual machine, permissions, and admin controls built into Cowork.

CrowdStrike’s Architectural Difference

AI agents don't operate in one layer, and neither does Falcon Guardian. Agents reach out over the network to communicate with LLMs, but they also execute processes locally on the workstations where they’re installed. These actions may never cross network boundaries. The Falcon sensor and Falcon Guardian see both agentic workstreams and fuse them together in a single view from CrowdStrike’s endpoint network inspection and OS-level visibility. This unified view, CrowdStrike® Agent Graph, shows analysts not only what agents were asked to do, but what they did at runtime.

CrowdStrike also delivers agent-level enforcement controls via hook integrations for agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

The Claude Cowork integration extends Falcon Guardian coverage to a new place agents work. It takes Falcon Guardian’s runtime security foundation into the VM where Cowork runs its code, providing visibility and detection for what the agent executes, installs, and connects to across its lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution.

What's Next

Endpoint agents like Claude Cowork run their code inside a VM that host-only security can't see into. By running the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM on macOS and Windows, this integration will close that gap. It will bring Falcon visibility and detection to where agents execute, it will be deployed and controlled through Falcon, and it will extend the runtime foundation of the three layers of AI security in Falcon Guardian.

The integration is focused on visibility and detection inside the VM. Available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November 2026, it enables customers to deploy the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM through their existing device management tools. Their teams gain visibility and detection across the processes, packages, and network activity inside the VM.

Title: What Makes a Good Security Agent? 5 Lessons from the AgentWorks Hackathon
Context: Working with NVIDIA, we launched the first AgentWorks Hackathon and invited security teams to nominate agents they’ve built
Full Text:
Every security team is being told to adopt AI. Far fewer have been shown what "good" looks like in practice. Turnkey agents handle common, well-defined security tasks, but no two security teams operate the same way. Each has its own data, playbooks, escalation paths, and risk tolerances; unique context that no vendor can anticipate in a packaged solution. That’s why we built CrowdStrike® Charlotte AI™ AgentWorks: a no-code workspace that lets every security team build the exact agents they need, on the Falcon platform.

The power of the crowd is one of the most enduring advantages we have as an industry against the adversary. What one analyst learns on the front lines, the whole community inherits. Now, adversaries are rapidly gaining AI fluency, and defenders need to transform the SOC the way we always have: together. When one team turns a hard problem into a working agent, it raises the bar for all of us. Every team can learn from that agent, adapt it, and build on it.

So, we summoned the ingenuity of the crowd like never before. Working with NVIDIA, we launched the first AgentWorks Hackathon and invited security teams to nominate agents they’ve built. The brief was wide open: each team picked its own problem and defined its build. Nearly a hundred nominations poured in from more than 50 countries, each aimed at a persistent bottleneck its builders knew firsthand and forged to earn its place as a trusted extension of the team.

The standouts went further. They were intentionally designed, governed by clear guardrails, and deliver real impact. Here are the winning agents and five lessons every security team can apply today.

Winner Spotlights

“Agent Smith”: Finding the MCP Servers Nobody Knew Were Running

AI coding tools can launch an MCP server on a developer laptop with a single command. Most security teams have no inventory of them. In one day, one company discovered 1,710 hosts running unapproved MCP servers, including a revoked server, unapproved mailbox readers, and one with TLS verification turned off. Nobody had been watching.

Agent Smith hunts these cases down. It finds MCP servers running on endpoints, checks each against the organization's approved list, and reads redacted command lines for risky settings. In doing so, it turns a blind spot into a daily inventory with a clear next step for every server.

The sophistication here wasn't just in the prompt. It was in the architecture: a deliberate division of labor between the model and deterministic tools like queries and workflows. That split sharpened accuracy and controlled cost.

Before the agent runs, an upstream query in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM does the heavy lifting, carrying the company's own context: signature rules encoding the approved tool list, noise filters tuned during testing, and host lookups mapping each server to a business unit. It also redacts sensitive data before handing the agent a command-line sample and package names.

The agent then gets to work: explaining what each server is, flagging risky settings (TLS off, unpinned versions, credentials on the command line), and recommending a next step based on the team's existing approval process (switch to an approved server, request a review, or register a custom build). Charlotte Agentic SOAR then passes that context into a new case for the governance team to review.

“Help Desk Takeover Defender” Agent: Catching MFA Reset Abuse in 70 Seconds

Multifactor authentication (MFA) exploitation is one of the most effective plays in the modern attacker's playbook: Call the service desk, impersonate an employee, get their MFA reset, register your own device, and walk into the account. The challenge for defenders is that a malicious reset can look almost exactly like a legitimate one.

The Help Desk Takeover Defender agent ensures every MFA reset is investigated for abuse within moments of a new reset. Manual investigations that previously took 20 to 30 minutes now run in about 70 seconds against live data, and containment drops from hours to minutes. It pulls Entra ID logs and the supporting Falcon telemetry behind a reset, then scores the likelihood of a social engineering attack. If the signs point to a takeover, it can revoke sessions, disable the user, or contain the host.

What earned this agent its recognition was how it balanced trust and speed. The scoring is deterministic, computed upstream by a CrowdStrike Falcon® Foundry function rather than the model, so the same evidence produces the same verdict. The model compares each reset against that user's 30-day history, then draws on knowledge files that encode the team's playbook: what's considered normal, how to verify a user with a callback, and which containment paths are warranted and when. No action happens without a human in the loop: Every containment step requires explicit approval and the approver's name on record.

“Exclusion Adversary” Agent: The Agent that Attacks its Own Work

Every security team manages exclusions: rules that tell security tools to stop alerting on recurring, harmless activity. But left unattended, exclusions can become blind spots of their own. A rule written too loosely doesn't just quiet the noise; it hides any real attack that happens to share the same pattern. A good exclusion has to thread the needle: wide enough to catch the noise, but tight enough that an attacker can't hide behind it.

The Exclusion Adversary agent turns that balancing act into a repeatable, evidence-backed step. It gathers live detection counts and drafts the narrowest exclusion that would safely apply. Then it does what analysts rarely have time for: It attacks its own draft. It lists every field the rule leaves wide open and writes bypass strings an adversary might use to slip through, such as a same-named binary dropped in a writable folder. It ends with a verdict and an approval checklist for an analyst to review.

What sets this agent apart is its adversarial mindset turned inward. Most agents try to be right. This one assumes it might be wrong and goes looking for proof. Its discipline caught a real defect in testing: The agent's first draft used a common wildcard pattern that matched a program by name in any folder. That meant an attacker could plant a lookalike elsewhere and the exclusion would silence it too. The agent flagged the gap and tightened the rule to the exact file path.

Notable Runners-Up

This is CQL Agent: Security queries can run without errors but still fail. AI-drafted detections are especially prone to this. This agent checks whether queries and detection rules work as intended. It takes output from CrowdStrike’s LogScale query assistant or the Falcon Next-Gen SIEM Correlation Rule Generation Agent and runs it through a fixed series of gates, including a check against a 196-function CrowdStrike Query Language (CQL) catalog, 23 silent-failure rules, and a reproducible unit test. Each one ends with a verdict: validated, validated with limits, or inconclusive. Judges singled out its reproducible tests and its willingness to return an inconclusive result. An agent that admits what it can't prove is one you can trust when it returns a "validated” verdict.

TaHiTI Threat Hunting Agent: Structured threat hunting can take a senior analyst hours; most of it spent on research, schema lookups, query debugging, and write-ups rather than hunting. This agent runs the full Targeted Hunting integrating Threat Intelligence (TaHiTI) methodology end-to-end. It scopes queries to keep costs under control and produces a standardized, ServiceNow-ready hunt record. The result: junior analysts can now run hunts that once waited on senior staff. The method stops living in one person's head and can be run by the whole team.

HOPSCOTCH Agent (Lateral Movement Flight Recorder): Tracing an identity or process across entry, internal hops, and exit points can be a time-consuming process. Given an account name, HOPSCOTCH reconstructs that entity’s path as a chronological, confidence-rated chain, corroborating source activity, authentication, destination execution, and post-arrival behavior at each hop. At each link, the agent provides supporting evidence and a confidence level, so analysts can see what it knows and what it’s inferring.

EASM Heartbeat Agent: An organization's external attack surface changes constantly. Each morning, the EASM Heartbeat agent emails the security team a short report on what changed across its external attack surface in the last 24 hours: new findings, new IPs, new “Critical” and “High” CVE misconfigurations, and which way the risk score is moving. One weekend, its findings more than doubled, tracing the spike to newly attributed assets carrying critical, actively used exploits. Its report revealed to the team that much of the inventory had never been reviewed, which led to a recurring asset review.

Dysfunctional Family-Tree Agent: Most attacks today are malware-free. To catch them, this agent proactively audits two- and three-generation process lineage (grandparent, parent, child) against a lookup table of patterns common to LOLBin attacks, decodes obfuscated command lines, and opens a case for medium-or-worse findings.

Hall Pass Agent: Security exemptions rarely expire on their own. One organization found more than 25,000 hosts carrying a USB exemption, with no active approval on record for over two years. The Hall Pass agent reconciles the exemptions the Falcon platform enforces against internal approval records, measures whether each is still used, and opens a renew-or-revoke case for the owner, so exceptions stay current and reviewed.

SneakerNet Agent: The Falcon sensor records every file written to USB, far too many for any team to review by hand. In a 30 day window, one team found merger documents, litigation holds, and pay statements copied to removable drives without triggering a single alert. Blocking USB would break legitimate work, so every hour a detection query flags sensitive files written to or opened from USB drives and SD cards. The agent scores each device, checking the machine’s role and whether the same drive has been on other hosts. It then opens a case for the data owner showing what left, how, and why it scored the way it did, without blocking anything or naming the user.

What Makes a Good Security Agent?

Five traits set apart the best agents:

They solve real problems: The best agents target the work that drains analyst time, or worse, the work that always loses to urgent tasks and never gets done. These problems aren't always glamorous, but they're often low-risk and high-return cases for automation. Moreover, the best builds didn't just move a bottleneck downstream or create new ones. They closed the gap, doing work that otherwise wouldn't happen.

They connect data, reasoning, and action, and plug into processes that teams already run: A good agent is defined by an architecture that applies AI reasoning exactly where judgment is needed and leans on other technologies for everything else. The strongest builds didn't make the model do everything. They made it do the one thing only a model can, then handed the rest to tools that are faster, cheaper, and deterministic, such as for routing, loops, query searches, and fixed calculations. They also structured outputs to hand off cleanly to the workflows, cases, and agents downstream.

They have built-in guardrails: The best builders treated trust as a design problem. They capped tool calls, retry limits, and per-run credits. They redacted sensitive data before the model ever saw it. They refused to let the model invent facts, or required a named human to approve any consequential action. The best of them made the dangerous action structurally impossible, such as instructing agents to disclose when information is incomplete or routing containment through workflows that require analyst approval. As one judge noted, “For a cyberdefense team, an agent’s ability to disclose missing evidence, avoid unsupported conclusions, and preserve human control matters as much as its speed.”

They drive measurable outcomes and improve over time: The top builds were designed around tasks that could be evaluated, then refined across versions and benchmarked against real or synthetic datasets until they met the required bar for accuracy. This is what separates a demo from a production-ready agent: one that can be measured and continuously optimized, earning the trust to graduate to more autonomous work.

They're creative: Some of the most memorable submissions weren't faster versions of existing work. They approached problems from entirely new angles: an agent that attacks detection exclusions to expose the blind spot, an agent that hunts down unauthorized agents. Some of the most forward-looking builds pointed at questions the industry is only beginning to ask, like whether an agent's activity isn’t just internally authorized but legal under local regulations.

Agent Traces: How the Best Agents Got Even Better

One last habit set the standout agents apart: They used AgentWorks agent traces to understand how their agent worked and to optimize its design.

Every time an AgentWorks agent runs, it leaves an execution trace, a step-by-step record of what the agent did: which tools it called, the exact query it sent, what came back, how long each step took, and how many credits each step consumed. The trace view is a powerful resource for troubleshooting and optimizing agent design. Builders noted how this helped them troubleshoot four common issues:

Errors the agent ignores: A tool errors out, and the agent either moves on or quietly substitutes different results, building a confident conclusion on missing data. The fix: Include explicit prompt instructions for how to handle errors, including never filling gaps with substitute data.

Zero rows misread as "none": No error appears, just an empty result. The agent reports "nothing found" when the real cause was a timeout or a query that never ran. The fix: Have the agent confirm the query completed before reporting "none," and report "not retrieved" if it can't. Then redesign the query, for example by narrowing the time window, rather than retrying it unchanged.

Over-chaining and wasted turns: Timeouts and excessive agent-to-agent chaining inflate latency and cost without improving accuracy. The fix: Trim the chain to the steps that actually improve the answer, and remove tools the agent doesn't need.

Knowledge bases that never got used: An agent is only as good as its context. Traces can also reveal when agents don’t open their attached knowledge base. The fix: Force a knowledge lookup on every run or encode knowledge as an agent skill.

Extending Threat Hunting and MDR to AI

As organizations increasingly connect AI systems to sensitive data, applications, and infrastructure, adversaries have new opportunities to exploit trusted access and legitimate AI capabilities. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, AI agents triggered 2.5 times more detection leads than human activity, underscoring how AI-driven activity is increasing the volume and velocity of signals threat hunters must assess.

Falcon Adversary OverWatch Cross-Domain now extends 24/7 proactive threat hunting to AI applications and autonomous agent activity monitored by CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian. By combining Falcon Guardian's runtime context with telemetry across the Falcon platform and frontline adversary intelligence, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters can uncover manipulation, abuse, and emerging adversary tradecraft that automated detections may miss. Every organization has a different threat profile. Industry, geography, infrastructure, business operations, and the broader technology ecosystem all influence which adversaries and threats matter most.

The challenge is putting threat intelligence to work at scale to identify the greatest threats to each business. The intelligence that security teams rely on is as varied as the threats they face. Organizations draw from commercial threat intelligence providers, industry information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs), government sources, open-source research, trusted partners, and indicators uncovered through their own threat hunting and incident response efforts.

Modern security operations need a "Bring your own intelligence" strategy to manage these disparate sources. CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings threat intelligence and security telemetry together in Third-Party IOC Management, a new feature that enables organizations to incorporate their own intelligence directly into detection and investigation workflows.

By centralizing the ingestion, curation, and lifecycle management of third-party indicators, security teams can operationalize the intelligence most relevant to their environment alongside CrowdStrike's adversary intelligence and telemetry from both the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform and third-party sources.

Turn Threat Intelligence into a Detection Advantage

Valuable indicators are often scattered across spreadsheets, ticketing tools, and threat intelligence platforms, which are often disconnected from the security telemetry that analysts rely on. Manually importing and maintaining indicators across multiple tools creates operational overhead. Limited real-time correlation and outdated indicators of compromise (IOCs) can delay threat detection, generate unnecessary alerts, and slow investigations.

Instead of manually moving indicators between disconnected tools, security teams can manage their intelligence within Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, reducing operational complexity and accelerating the path from threat intelligence to actionable security insights.

Figure 1. See how Third-Party IOC Management in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM helps security teams ingest, manage, and correlate their own threat intelligence with security telemetry to accelerate detection and investigation.

Third-Party IOC Management helps eliminate the operational barriers that slow detection and investigation through four key capabilities:

Eliminates manual IOC onboarding: Ingest and manage third-party IOCs, including IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, from commercial intelligence providers, industry sharing communities, and internal investigations. With support for STIX/TAXII, APIs, and direct uploads, security teams can streamline intelligence onboarding, automatically consolidate duplicate indicators across sources, and reduce the effort required to maintain intelligence across disparate tools.

Accelerates detection and threat hunting: Put third-party intelligence to work in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM through curated indicator lists that are automatically updated. Security teams can use these indicators in correlation rules and threat hunting searches to identify known malicious infrastructure and suspicious activity across security telemetry, accelerating detection and investigation without manually maintaining separate indicator lists.

Reduces alert noise with automated IOC lifecycle management: Maintain control over third-party indicators with expiration settings and management capabilities that help prevent outdated intelligence from creating unnecessary noise. By keeping IOC collections current and relevant, security teams can reduce manual maintenance, minimize false positives associated with stale indicators, and focus investigations on threats that matter.

Expands detection coverage with organization-specific intelligence: Extend CrowdStrike's adversary intelligence and AI-native detection capabilities with intelligence specific to your organization. By bringing third-party and proprietary indicators together with CrowdStrike intelligence and security telemetry, teams can broaden detection coverage and investigate threats with context that reflects both the global threat landscape and their unique environment.

To see how these capabilities can work together in practice, consider a common industry-specific threat intelligence scenario. A financial services organization receives indicators associated with a targeted phishing campaign from an industry information-sharing community. With Third-Party IOC Management, the security team can bring these indicators into Falcon, consolidate duplicates, and manage their lifecycle while using them in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM to search security telemetry and build correlation rules to identify potentially related activity. This turns industry-specific intelligence into actionable detection and investigation context without manually distributing indicators across disconnected tools.

Connect Intelligence to Accelerate Security Operations

With Third-Party IOC Management built into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, organizations can maximize existing threat intelligence investments while reducing the complexity of maintaining disconnected tools and integrations. Rather than replacing the intelligence sources they rely on, security teams can bring that intelligence into the platform where they detect and investigate threats.

This consolidation also reduces the operational burden on analysts and detection engineers. Fewer manual handoffs, less context switching, and centralized IOC management mean teams can spend less time maintaining intelligence workflows and more time identifying suspicious activity, investigating threats, and taking action.

As security operations evolve toward the agentic SOC, the quality of AI-driven investigations and decisions will increasingly depend on access to relevant, timely, and contextualized security data. AI agents need more than telemetry alone; they need intelligence that helps explain what suspicious activity means within an organization's unique threat landscape.

By bringing third-party IOCs together with CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence and security telemetry in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, organizations can reduce data fragmentation and build a richer foundation for AI-driven security operations. This convergence creates opportunities for AI agents to correlate indicators with security events, enrich investigations with threat context, and support faster, more informed response decisions.

For supported agents, Falcon Guardian agent hooks bring even more detail into Agent Graph.

Agent hooks plug into an agent's native hooks system to capture activity at key points in a session: when a prompt is submitted, before a tool call runs, and after it completes. Title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign
Context: Where CrowdStrike has previously observed threat actors use AI agents to assist individual intrusions, VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to run multiple engagements simultaneously,...
Full Text:
CrowdStrike OverWatch identified a VAPOR PANDA campaign using ARTEX alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM to conduct intrusions against multiple high-value targets in parallel.

Beginning on October 17, 2026, the adversary used ARTEX against more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions.

The VAPOR PANDA campaign detailed in this blog post is separate from the ARTEX activity recently reported by industry sources under the Storm-0940 designation.1 CrowdStrike has previously documented ARTEX and similar agentic frameworks in use by financially motivated and unattributed actors; in this campaign, a targeted intrusion adversary used ARTEX to run parallel intrusions against multiple high-value targets. CrowdStrike Falcon telemetry also revealed details absent from public ARTEX reporting, including VAPOR PANDA's deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.2

This campaign marks an escalation in China-nexus use of AI agents, from single intrusions to multiple simultaneous engagements directed by a human operator. The operation also shows the adversary building endpoint sensor evasion directly into their agentic workflow, including instructions to identify hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor.

Details

Targeting

Beginning October 17, 2026, CrowdStrike OverWatch observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against entities in at least 14 countries over an 11-day window. The controller, which CrowdStrike Intelligence has linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure, intermittently exposed adversary tooling, target files, and ARTEX agent transcripts. This indicates multiple engagements (referred to as “tasks” by ARTEX) against multiple targets.

VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to conduct extensive intrusions at the foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, likely compromised a third, and staged target files for use against foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. The adversary also compromised a Middle East-based interior ministry. One engagement focused on a single European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, as well as defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities. A separate engagement targeted 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors. The adversary also compromised telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines.

CrowdStrike Intelligence confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations, where the adversary gained access, deployed BLOODALCHEMY, and conducted follow-on credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. The adversary also conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe.

Inside the Operation

VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM, supplemented with a second, subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not confirm. In a single intrusion, VAPOR PANDA’s planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole.

The campaign's reliance on open source components layered on top of commercial LLM subscriptions illustrates how adversaries can assemble scalable, multi-agent intrusions largely from publicly available resources. ARTEX coordinates a main agent with subordinate planner and worker agents over a shared graph of facts, findings, and goals, advancing each engagement from initial access through host reconnaissance and lateral movement. The framework kept a human in the loop: Recovered transcripts showed an operator issuing instructions in Chinese — marked with the label 【人类指令】 ("human instruction") and timestamped in China Standard Time — and directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and inventory endpoint sensor coverage.

Where CrowdStrike has previously observed threat actors use AI agents to assist individual intrusions, VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to run multiple engagements simultaneously, intervening only to steer the agents at decision points. The recovered transcripts and staged tooling show an adversary pairing AI-driven workflow with well-established tradecraft:

At a U.S.-based pharmaceutical organization, the agent chained an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service, obtaining a role capable of issuing administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating to recover an enterprise administrator account.

At a second U.S.-based pharmaceutical organization, the agent deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, read Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and abused resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account.

Against a Greek government entity, the operator supplied the agent with a 2022 directory export from the organization's mail server containing authentication keys that had likely not been rotated since the export. The agent used those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes, then used VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, alongside a VPN client key the operator described as originating from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network.

Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure. They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations.

VAPOR PANDA was also observed directing the agents to evade endpoint defenses. At a global pharmaceutical organization, the operator instructed the agents to “在域里寻找没有装猎鹰的windows机器，从tasklist和文件夹目录判断” (English translation: "find Windows machines in the domain without Falcon, judging by tasklist and folder listings"), using 猎鹰, which is People’s Republic of China (PRC) red-team slang for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. Incorporating sensor coverage checks directly into the agentic workflow allows the adversary to concentrate follow-on activity on unprotected hosts.

BLOODALCHEMY

At a Middle East-based interior ministry and a Latin America-based foreign ministry, VAPOR PANDA deployed BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor first publicly documented in October 2023. The adversary used a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe to load a malicious DLL, graphics-hook-filter64.dll, which decrypted the BLOODALCHEMY payload file graphics-hook_config.bin. The adversary staged copies of all three files in the exposed open directories. The implant carries an internal project path, D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\, that likely reflects the malware's in-house development name.

Across the observed activity, BLOODALCHEMY communicated with VAPOR PANDA infrastructure.These indicators do not appear in prior public ARTEX reporting and are also consolidated in the IOC table at the end of this post.

Assessment

This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation, likely indicating the AI-based framework is quickly gaining popularity among multiple China-nexus adversaries.

Since 2021, VAPOR PANDA has primarily targeted government, think tank, energy, and extractive organizations across Europe, North America, Oceania, and the UK to develop long-term access. This campaign marks the adversary's first observed use of AI-driven intrusion tooling and a notable broadening of its targeting into the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear, and defense sectors, as well as foreign ministries, across new regions. Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission. The operation’s reliance on DeepSeek and additional commercial LLMs, run through a purpose-built harness, likely reflects a deliberate effort to construct a resilient toolchain from multiple model providers rather than depend on any single service.

China-nexus adversaries will highly likely continue adopting agentic frameworks such as ARTEX over the next 12 months, pairing them with commercially available LLMs, and enabling small teams to quickly scale intrusions across many targets simultaneously.

Recommendations

Rotate signing keys, preauthentication keys, and service credentials after any suspected data exposure, including keys contained in historical backups and directory exports.

Enforce SAML signature validation, require IMDSv2, and restrict cloud roles' command-execution permissions to the minimum required instances.

Hunt for ARTEX markers, including command-line parameters containing artx or artex strings, artx-prefixed cloud roles, art18- administration-command comments, and the C:\ProgramData\artx5v\ directory.

Patch internet-facing appliances, particularly long-lived Linux-based servers, and ensure they run the latest available software and firmware.

Deploy an advanced, real-time endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent, such as the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, across the environment, including on servers considered inaccessible from the public internet.
